samples.summary: The CLI consent gate's central claim — "stops an unconfirmed CLI start before GitHub" — is never asserted: passport's `canActivate` is stubbed but no test checks it wasn't called
samples.evidence: `beforeEach` (line 108-113) does `jest.spyOn(passportBase, 'canActivate').mockReturnValue(true)` but never keeps a handle on the spy, and the only `not.toHaveBeenCalled()` in the whole file is on the logger warn (line 835). The test `it('stops an unconfirmed CLI start before GitHub')` asserts `guard.canActivate(context)).toBe(true)` — which is exactly what the mocked super returns, so it holds whether or not the guard short-circuits — plus `req.__oauthState` being undefined. A regression where the guard rendered the consent page AND still fell through to `super.canActivate(context)` (redirecting the victim to GitHub with no state, the exact forced-login/CLI-phish case the gate exists for) would leave every assertion in the file green. Same for the controller-side test `'does nothing for an ordinary start (the guard already redirected)'`, which only checks `res.send` was not called.

verdict.reason:
I could not find a single counterexample anywhere in the repo. The only spy on passport's `canActivate` is the anonymous one in `beforeEach` (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:107-113) — `jest.spyOn(passportBase, 'canActivate').mockReturnValue(true)` with no handle kept — and the sole `not.toHaveBeenCalled()` in that file is on the logger (line 835). I grepped the whole auth directory for `not.toHaveBeenCalled`/`toHaveBeenCalledTimes(0)` (only res/userService/warn assertions, none on passport), grepped every `*.spec.ts` for `canActivate|authenticate|github.com`, checked `github.strategy.spec.ts` (it stubs the *strategy's* base `authenticate`, never the guard's super), checked all of `packages/backend/test/*.e2e-spec.ts` (no `/auth/github` exercise; only env setup in test/helpers/integration-helpers.ts:94), and confirmed `GitHubAuthGuard` is referenced only in guard.ts, guard.spec.ts, auth.module.ts and auth.controller.ts.

The gap is real and exploitable by a plausible regression. The existing assertions in `it('stops an unconfirmed CLI start before GitHub')` do catch one variant: dropping the `return true` at github-auth.guard.ts:573 would let control reach the state-minting block (lines 587-593), so `expect(req.__oauthState).toBeUndefined()` (spec:394) and `expect(cookies).toHaveLength(1)` (spec:402) would go red. But replacing `return true` with `return super.canActivate(context)` — the exact case the gate exists for — leaves `__oauthState` undefined, one confirm cookie, and the mocked super returning `true`, so every assertion in the file stays green while the victim is redirected to GitHub. And that redirect really would go out unbound: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` omits `state` entirely when the guard set none (github.strategy.ts:61-68, pinned by github.strategy.spec.ts:172-176). The controller-side test only asserts `res.send` was not called (auth.controller.spec.ts:663-667), which says nothing about the guard. So the central claimed behavior ("never delegates to passport for an unconfirmed CLI start") has no assertion — a missing test for a new security-critical behavior, in this lens's lane.

finding.summary: No test covers that COOKIE_SECURE now decides `cliLoginAvailable` — the CLI consent gate on a plain-http, non-loopback origin
finding.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable` (github-auth.guard.ts:215) is `secureCookies(...) || loopbackCallback(...)`, so the new `COOKIE_SECURE` short-circuit in `secureCookies` (line 159-160) newly makes a CLI login startable on a plain-http non-loopback origin (COOKIE_SECURE=true) and newly *refuses* one on an https origin (COOKIE_SECURE=false). The existing gate tests use only `insecureConfig()`/`httpsConfig()` (spec lines 444-466, 686-700); the three new COOKIE_SECURE tests assert only `secureCookies()`'s return, `loginCookieName`, and the web state cookie's `secure` option. Nothing exercises `canActivate` with a CLI query under an overridden config, so a regression in either direction of that gate would pass green.

verdict.reason: Verified independently. `secureCookies` short-circuits on COOKIE_SECURE (github-auth.guard.ts:158-160) and `cliLoginAvailable` (github-auth.guard.ts:215-216) feeds the CLI consent gate that throws in `canActivate` (github-auth.guard.ts:518-522), so COOKIE_SECURE now flips whether a CLI login can start on a plain-http non-loopback origin (true) and refuses one on an https origin (false). Repo-wide grep for COOKIE_SECURE turns up exactly one test file; its three COOKIE_SECURE tests (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:747-798) assert only secureCookies()'s return, loginCookieName(), and — in the single canActivate call at :764-766 — a web-flow cookie's `secure` option, with no `mode: 'cli'` query. The CLI gate tests (spec:444-454 via insecureConfig(), spec:459-466 via the loopback default) use configs whose `get` returns undefined for COOKIE_SECURE (spec:26-57). Grep for `cliLoginAvailable`, `Command-line`, `requires an https server`, `secureCookies`, and `loginCookieName` finds no other spec or e2e file (auth.controller.spec.ts CLI hits are consent-page HTML only; packages/backend/test/*.e2e-spec.ts has none). So the newly reachable behavior — CLI start permitted/refused by COOKIE_SECURE — has no covering test in either direction; that is a behavior change with zero meaningful coverage, in-lane and major for this rubric.
